title: Who should care for our public spaces?
label: 17 November 2026 · Public spaces
summary: The committee explored how well-maintained public spaces affect people’s sense of safety, belonging and hope, and how residents can help shape and care for them. The witnesses argued that communities need a genuine say from the start, trusted local organisations need long-term support, and councils must continue essential services rather than leaving volunteers to fill gaps. Members also questioned how to make community-led funding realistic, lasting and accountable. The discussion highlighted a need for flexible funding, better evaluation and closer working between councils and local groups.

glossary.definition: People’s ability to influence decisions and take action in their community.

Money for buildings, equipment or other lasting assets.

Planning a project together with the people who will use or be affected by it.

chapters.title: Why cared-for places matter
chapters.takeaway: A well-kept public space can help people feel valued, but lasting pride grows when residents have a say in what happens there.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What difference does a well-maintained public space make to the people who live nearby?

turns.speaker: Mark Webb
turns.text: When people in Great Grimsby walk past boarded-up shops or neglected green spaces, it reinforces the feeling that nobody cares about their town—or their future. That can affect how young people feel about school and their prospects.

turns.speaker: Mark Webb
turns.text: But improving a place can change how people behave towards it. We put planters on the high street. One day, someone dropped a cigarette butt into one, and people sitting at a nearby pub stood up and said, “That’s our planter.” They’d begun to look after something they felt belonged to them.

turns.speaker: Rosie Apperley
turns.text: People need to feel that their area is cared for if we want them to take an active part in their community. In Nag’s Head, a fire-damaged building was left for months and a busy pedestrian crossing stayed closed. Residents felt the council didn’t care whether they could cross safely.

turns.speaker: Rosie Apperley
turns.text: People also felt that if the same thing happened in a more affluent part of Islington, it would be dealt with faster. Whether that’s objectively true or not, that’s how residents experienced it.

turns.speaker: Dr Joseph Owen
turns.text: Fixing benches, bins and other things matters, but we should also think about how people use a place and whether they feel safe and connected there. Tidying a space by itself won’t necessarily make people proud of it.

turns.speaker: Dr Joseph Owen
turns.text: I once asked Portsmouth City Council to put benches at the top of a local park, where people could enjoy the view. When I returned and saw them, I felt I’d helped make something happen. People were using them, and I felt a stronger connection to the park.

turns.speaker: Dr Joseph Owen
turns.text: Someone later complained online that a bench had been marked with graffiti. I saw that as evidence that young people were using it. Public spaces are used in different ways, and their meaning isn’t always simple.

turns.speaker: Lord Bailey of Paddington
turns.text: Some people worry that volunteers or more affluent residents take over spaces that were built for working-class communities. Others say local people damage spaces themselves. How do we know residents want to look after them?

turns.speaker: Rosie Apperley
turns.text: We’re working with residents on housing estates who want green spaces they can use. They’re more likely to care for a place if they help design and create it, and learn how to look after it.

turns.speaker: Rosie Apperley
turns.text: But residents shouldn’t be left to do everything. Council services still need to collect bins and deal with basic maintenance. People want to know that the council is doing its part too.

turns.speaker: Mark Webb
turns.text: You can’t do things for a community without involving it from the beginning. We renovated an old social club on a deprived estate, but it was repeatedly vandalised while it sat empty.

turns.speaker: Mark Webb
turns.text: A woman from the estate took it on as a business. She knew the people responsible for the damage and told them to leave it alone. The vandalism stopped almost overnight, and residents began planting around the building.

turns.speaker: Mark Webb
turns.text: That doesn’t mean one group should be set against another. Residents, volunteers, councils and businesses should all help decide what the area needs.

chapters.title: Funding that starts with local needs
chapters.takeaway: Funding works better when residents help set priorities before a project is designed, and when they have time and support to show what changed.

turns.speaker: Baroness Lawrence of Clarendon
turns.text: How could government funding for local spaces be improved?

turns.speaker: Dr Joseph Owen
turns.text: Some earlier programmes didn’t create lasting change. Our research on one towns programme found that many people making decisions were white and over 50, so they didn’t necessarily represent the places the money was meant to help.

turns.speaker: Dr Joseph Owen
turns.text: Another funding programme focused heavily on building work, rather than the local organisations and people needed to keep spaces active. Pride in Place offers longer-term funding, but most of it still appears to be for buildings and other physical improvements.

turns.speaker: Dr Joseph Owen
turns.text: Give communities more choice over how much they spend on buildings and how much on staff and activities. Help them plan projects together with residents, and measure whether people feel more able to influence what happens in their area.

turns.speaker: Rosie Apperley
turns.text: Bring local organisations in from the start. Community centres already have trusted relationships with residents; an outside group can’t just ask them to bring people into a meeting after all the decisions have been made.

turns.speaker: Mark Webb
turns.text: Often, the process starts with an available pot of money and a set of measures, and then organisations write bids around those rules. Instead, first ask residents what their area needs and be honest about what can and can’t be done. Then decide what money is available and how to measure the results.

turns.speaker: Baroness Lawrence of Clarendon
turns.text: Projects can lose their funding before they’ve had time to take root. How long should support last?

turns.speaker: Mark Webb
turns.text: For major, lasting changes, ten years should be the minimum. That takes the work beyond an election cycle. Local groups and public servants need to be involved from the start so the work can continue as elected leaders change.

turns.speaker: Baroness Andrews
turns.text: There was a ten-year community programme in the early 2000s. What can we learn from it, and how can we tell whether Pride in Place has worked?

turns.speaker: Dr Joseph Owen
turns.text: We need to begin measuring early. I don’t know whether Pride in Place has money set aside for evaluation, but without a starting point it’ll be hard to say what has changed over ten years.

turns.speaker: Dr Joseph Owen
turns.text: The local boards were set up quickly, and places made different choices about how much residents helped shape the board itself. That could affect who gets a say later, when the spending plan is decided.

turns.speaker: Baroness Griffin of Princethorpe
turns.text: How can projects measure ideas like pride and agency over the long term?

turns.speaker: Dr Joseph Owen
turns.text: Pride can mean different things in different places, so it’s difficult to measure with one standard number. Ask residents what matters to them, then compare their answers over time alongside other measures. It won’t be perfect, but it can show whether their experience is changing.

turns.speaker: Rosie Apperley
turns.text: Small organisations often have no time or money for research. Funders may expect them to promise exact results before they’ve had a chance to listen to residents. We need researchers to help develop simple ways for community groups and councils to track progress.

turns.speaker: Mark Webb
turns.text: Don’t impose measures before a community has decided what it needs. Ask the group how it will show whether the project worked, and make that part of its plan.

chapters.title: Volunteers need support, not extra burdens
chapters.takeaway: Community groups can help care for local places, but they need councils to provide essential services, respect their work and make it easier to coordinate.

turns.speaker: Baroness Janke
turns.text: Volunteers can improve a park but may not be able to stop damage or organise how others use it. How should they work with councils and the police?

turns.speaker: Mark Webb
turns.text: Public agencies should help residents do good work, not make it harder. Volunteers don’t always need payment; they need to be listened to, valued and given practical support. If they need more authority, connect them with the agencies that have it.

turns.speaker: Baroness Janke
turns.text: What if a council books an event on a garden that volunteers maintain, and the event damages the plants they’ve paid for and planted?

turns.speaker: Rosie Apperley
turns.text: There should be a clear way for groups to register land they care for, so councils check with them before arranging events. Council departments also need to communicate: the staff treating trees or plants need to know what residents have planted.

turns.speaker: Rosie Apperley
turns.text: Local organisations can help explain decisions too. If the council explains why a tree can’t be planted in a particular spot, residents are more likely to understand than if they simply hear “no”.

turns.speaker: Rosie Apperley
turns.text: We’re trying to bring Islington Council departments together with community groups so residents can discuss practical limits directly. That kind of coordination often doesn’t happen.

turns.speaker: Baroness Janke
turns.text: Volunteer groups can fade when parents return to work or older volunteers become less able to take part. How can local projects survive?

turns.speaker: Rosie Apperley
turns.text: A long-standing local organisation can help keep a project going when particular volunteers leave. Groups also need to keep welcoming new people, rather than becoming closed circles.

turns.speaker: Dr Joseph Owen
turns.text: People volunteer for different reasons. Some want work experience, while others have more time after retirement. We should understand those reasons, but also avoid asking community organisations to replace services they aren’t equipped to provide.

turns.speaker: Baroness Andrews
turns.text: Could councils pay local organisations to maintain spaces instead of awarding contracts to large companies?

turns.speaker: Rosie Apperley
turns.text: That’s possible through a service-level agreement. One Islington community centre has been paid to look after a local orchard. The centre can involve residents, rather than having a contractor arrive with no connection to the neighbourhood.

turns.speaker: Lord Bailey of Paddington
turns.text: There’s a risk that if community groups take on public services, they become part of government and lose their independence. What should they be expected to do, and what must remain the council’s job?

turns.speaker: Rosie Apperley
turns.text: There needs to be a basic level of council service. Community groups shouldn’t be asked to take over just because the council can’t afford to do its job. It works better when residents want to create something new and choose to help care for it.

turns.speaker: Mark Webb
turns.text: First work out what needs doing, then decide who can do it best. Sometimes that’ll be the council; sometimes a local group. Groups also need a realistic plan and budget, rather than being expected to do more than they can.

turns.speaker: Rosie Apperley
turns.text: It depends on the task. In one project, the council is doing the building work to improve drainage, while our organisation is listening to residents and involving them in planting. We can share the work rather than draw a rigid line between us.

turns.speaker: Dr Joseph Owen
turns.text: Planning with residents and building local organisations takes longer, and may cost more at the start. But if the plan doesn’t fit what people need, the change may be short-lived and people won’t feel involved.

chapters.title: Local leadership, public investment and political risk
chapters.takeaway: National and local investment can help, but it needs to complement local knowledge and must not raise hopes beyond what can realistically be delivered.

turns.speaker: Lord Ravensdale
turns.text: How can the more locally led approaches you’ve described work across the country, rather than in just a few places?

turns.speaker: Mark Webb
turns.text: Give each area time—perhaps a year or 18 months—to listen to residents and prepare a plan before discussing the money. Then fund what’s feasible, and let the community that developed the plan help make decisions.

turns.speaker: Rosie Apperley
turns.text: Listening first is essential. We spent 18 months talking with residents about what nature they wanted in their neighbourhood. We now have a plan we’re delivering with the council and the National Trust.

turns.speaker: Rosie Apperley
turns.text: Councils should also have a way to share what works, so each place doesn’t have to invent its own processes from scratch.

turns.speaker: Dr Joseph Owen
turns.text: One useful idea is to train residents to research what their neighbours need. Universities and organisations such as the Local Government Association could share guides and materials, even if it isn’t possible to fund a research team in every area.

turns.speaker: Baroness Andrews
turns.text: Voluntary organisations are often short of staff and time. What practical change would help them?

turns.speaker: Rosie Apperley
turns.text: Councils need to trust local groups to work with residents and pay them for that work, rather than keeping everything in-house. A local group may be better placed to knock on doors than a council acting as landlord.

turns.speaker: Lord Cameron of Dillington
turns.text: Can investment in historic buildings transform a market town just as much as residents organising from the bottom up?

turns.speaker: Mark Webb
turns.text: It can help, but towns also need to adapt to what people use them for now. High streets can be places to meet and do things, not just shop. If useful spaces aren’t opened up, empty units can be taken by businesses residents didn’t ask for.

turns.speaker: Mark Webb
turns.text: Local pop-up shops, reduced business costs and support for new businesses can help. Once one place opens, nearby businesses may follow. I’d rather see local businesses lead than national chains.

turns.speaker: Dr Joseph Owen
turns.text: Investment in historic buildings can make people feel that their town is improving. But a project can also miss the mark. In Darlington, some old town-centre buildings were painted in a way local people didn’t feel represented their town’s history.

turns.speaker: Dr Joseph Owen
turns.text: Big building projects and community-led work can complement each other. But if people feel a project has been imposed on them, it may not build a sense of ownership.

turns.speaker: Lord Porter of Spalding
turns.text: If residents are invited to ask for things without knowing what can be funded, they may be disappointed and blame local politicians when promises aren’t met. How do you stop that happening?

turns.speaker: Mark Webb
turns.text: Be honest at the start about what can and can’t be done. People understand limits if you explain them. The trouble is promising something that can’t be delivered, not asking the community what it wants.

turns.speaker: Lord Porter of Spalding
turns.text: But local politics in Grimsby has changed hands repeatedly. That suggests people may lose faith when promises aren’t kept.

turns.speaker: Mark Webb
turns.text: I don’t agree that political changes have stopped our work. We’ve kept working through changes in local leadership. Community projects can last beyond election cycles if they belong to the people who live there.

turns.speaker: Lord Bassam of Brighton
turns.text: Can moving government jobs to towns help local businesses and communities?

turns.speaker: Dr Joseph Owen
turns.text: It can make a difference, but it isn’t a cure-all. In Darlington, some people working at the government site travel from London and spend money in the town centre, but people living nearby may still feel that the centre isn’t for them.

turns.speaker: Rosie Apperley
turns.text: Community centres are already providing meals and warm spaces to people who can’t afford to heat their homes. That’s important work, but those organisations need funding for their own basic costs too.

turns.speaker: Mark Webb
turns.text: Public money doesn’t have to mean more spending. We’ve used an initial investment to build a social enterprise that has provided business support for 15 years. If you plan properly, some early spending can make later work sustainable.

chapters.title: What the witnesses would change
chapters.takeaway: The witnesses called for genuine local influence, investment in the people and organisations that sustain places, and plans that are realistic and accountable.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: If you could make one change tomorrow, what would you do?

turns.speaker: Dr Joseph Owen
turns.text: Whenever you improve a physical space, invest in the people, organisations and activities that will keep it meaningful. Bring communities in early enough to shape the plan, and give them real choices within the available budget.

turns.speaker: Rosie Apperley
turns.text: I’d make sure every neighbourhood had a paid community organiser to help residents work together and have a say.

turns.speaker: Mark Webb
turns.text: Give every town time to hear what residents want and prepare a realistic, evidence-based plan. Then decide what can be funded and hold both the council and the community to their commitments.
